extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), USPTO OED staff, and administrative adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedural standards used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to determine (a) entry of default judgment for failure to answer, (b) whether practitioner conduct violates the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility, and (c) appropriate sanctions. Includes service rules, statutory/regulatory violations, sanctioning factors, and aggravating/mitigating considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer — default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in default judgment. 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner who does not file a timely answer after proper service is deemed to have admitted the complaint's allegations; the OED Director may move for entry of default judgment and the court may grant it. In this case the Default Motion was GRANTED and the practitioner's admissions were deemed to include all factual allegations in the Complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by publication and computation of answer deadline (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When service cannot be accomplished pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2)(i), the OED may serve by notice via publication pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b). The OED Director caused an appropriate notice to be published in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If served by publication the time for filing an answer is thirty days from the second publication of the notice. Publication dates and the computation (e.g., changing an initial deadline) are determinative of the answer deadline used to assess timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct; duty to notify client (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a),(b),(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a), a "practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct." § 10.23(b)(5) provides that "a practitioner shall not [e]ngage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice." § 10.23(c)(5) proscribes "[f]ailing to inform a client or former client or failing to timely notify the Office of an inability to notify a client or former client of correspondence received from the Office ... when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client or former client and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client or former client should be notified."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: failing to inform clients of Notices to File Missing Parts, non-final Office actions, and Notices of Abandonment. The three-part test in § 10.23(c)(5) (significant effect; received on behalf of client; reasonable practitioner would notify) is used to decide when notification is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of legal matter (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c), "a practitioner shall not [n]eglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect includes failing to respond to Office communications, failing to respond to client inquiries, and allowing patent applications to become abandoned without client knowledge or consent. Such neglect supports disciplinary conclusions under § 10.77(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on intentional or habitual violation (37 C.F.R. § 10.59(c)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 10.59(c)(6), a practitioner shall not intentionally or habitually violate the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failures (e.g., multiple abandoned applications across clients due to the same conduct) support a finding of intentional or habitual violation and weigh toward more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on other conduct reflecting poorly on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6), "a practitioner shall not [e]ngage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulation is a catch-all for conduct that diminishes a practitioner's fitness; the OED must allege such conduct to obtain a violation under this subsection (the Court found no basis to find a § 10.23(b)(6) violation here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific practitioner acts constituting violations (communicative and performance failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific acts identified as misconduct include: failing to inform clients of Notices to File Missing Parts, non-final Office actions, and Notices of Abandonment; allowing applications to become abandoned without client knowledge or consent; knowingly misrepresenting that "everything was OK" with applications; failing to return client telephone calls; and providing factually inaccurate status information to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete behaviors are treated as evidence of violations of the above regulatory provisions (e.g., § 10.23(c)(5), § 10.77(c), § 10.59(c)(6)). They also show the types of conduct that cause client injury (loss of patent rights, extra fees to revive applications) and thus inform sanctioning decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED investigations (failure to respond to Requests for Information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent received Requests for Information (RFIs) dated February 8, 2013 and March 15, 2013 and failed to respond. Respondent later acknowledged receipt and requested an extension but then failed to respond by the extended date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to OED RFIs is cited as a separate neglect/cooperation failure relevant to discipline and can be considered in assessing culpability and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider before imposing sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.84(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner the Court must consider: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a Client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.84(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies each factor: duty violated (yes — duty to clients/profession), state of mind (found knowing/intentionally by default), injury (actual client harm and extra fees), and aggravating/mitigating factors (see ABA Standards guidance). The combination of these factors can support a range of sanctions up to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions to evaluate aggravating/mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court often looks to the ABA's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when determining whether aggravating or mitigating factors exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of aggravating factors recognized here: (a) prior disciplinary offense (recent OED warning letter addressing identical misconduct), (b) substantial experience in the practice of law (nearly 40 years, indicating knowledge of obligations), and (c) a pattern of misconduct and multiple offenses (numerous abandoned applications across many clients). These factors supported a maximum sanction (exclusion) in this matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences where all factors support maximum sanction (exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner has violated duties to clients and the profession, acted knowingly/intentionally, caused actual harm, and aggravating factors exist (e.g., prior disciplinary action, substantial experience, pattern of misconduct), the Court may impose the maximum sanction, including exclusion from practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision concludes that, based on deemed admissions and analysis of the four sanctioning factors, exclusion (bar from practice before the USPTO in all matters) is warranted and ordered. Prior remedial opportunities (e.g., prior warning letter) and subsequent client injuries (fees, lost rights) are weighed toward exclusion.
